opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, actually. When I joined, we were a very small group, and the whole idea from the start, coming from David and Llion, was that we wanted to do research that was a bit different from what the big labs were doing. Not just scaling up the same transformer recipe with more compute, but drawing inspiration from nature: evolution, collective intelligence, self-organization, these kinds of ideas.

As we've grown, I'd say the core spirit has stayed surprisingly intact, and part of that is deliberate. We still try to give researchers a lot of freedom to follow their curiosity. There's this sense that you should work on something that, if it works, would be genuinely surprising, rather than something that's a guaranteed incremental improvement. Things like evolutionary model merging, the AI Scientist work, or more recently the continuous thought machines: those all came from people being allowed to take a bit of a weird bet.

Of course, growth brings tension. We now have business partnerships, especially in Japan, and there's real applied work happening with banks and other industry partners. So there's a natural pull between exploration and exploitation, to use the RL framing. But I actually think that's healthy. The applied side grounds us and gives us real problems, and the research side keeps us from becoming just another consultancy that fine-tunes models.

For me personally, what makes it work is that the bar for "interesting" hasn't dropped. People still get excited in Slack about a strange result from some small experiment. As long as that curiosity-driven culture survives, I think we're in a good place. The hard part is protecting it as we keep scaling, and that's something we have to keep actively choosing.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes pursuing unconventional, curiosity-driven ideas, but does not clearly say these ideas receive relatively little research support across the broader machine-learning community.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so, I mean, this is something that I actually think about a lot, because when we started it was, you know, a handful of people, and the whole premise was kind of this nature-inspired, bottom-up view of intelligence. The name itself, Sakana, is fish, and the idea was a school of fish — lots of small, simple things that together do something smarter than any individual. And I think the question as you scale is whether you can keep that spirit when you're no longer a school of five fish but, you know, a much bigger organization with customers and a Tokyo office and all of that.

And honestly, what I'd say is that the spirit has stayed pretty intact, maybe surprisingly so. A big part of that is that the leadership really came out of research. David and Llion and Ren, they're not people who think of research as a cost center. The bet from the beginning was that if you let people follow their curiosity, and you give them compute and a bit of freedom, interesting things come out, and some of those things end up being useful. Evolutionary model merging is a good example of that, right? That started as a sort of, "huh, what if we don't train from scratch, what if we just recombine what's already out there?" — very much in the collective-intelligence, nature-inspired vein — and it ended up being something the company could actually build on.

The AI Scientist is maybe the other example I'd point to, and that one's close to my heart. That started as a fairly wild question — can you automate the whole research loop, ideation, experiments, writing, review — and the first version was, let's be honest, a bit of a toy. But the fact that we were allowed to push it to the point where a paper actually went through peer review, that tells you something about the culture. Nobody said, "okay, that's cute, now go do something that makes money."

Now, I don't want to be naive about it. As you grow, there's more structure. There's more engineering, there's more talk about products and about the Japanese market specifically, and that's healthy — a lab that only writes papers doesn't survive. The way I think about it is that the research side is kind of the exploration budget. You want a lot of small, cheap experiments, most of which fail, and you don't want to kill them too early. And I think the thing we've tried to protect is exactly that: small teams, fast iteration, a lot of open-sourcing, and a willingness to work on ideas that are slightly unfashionable — evolution, artificial life, continuous-time models — rather than just doing the next scaled-up transformer.

So, if anything, my hope is that growth lets us be more ambitious on the weird ideas, not less, because now there's a bit more runway to let them mature. But it's a thing you have to actively defend. It doesn't happen by default.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Sakana has been willing to pursue “slightly unfashionable” ideas such as evolution, artificial life, and continuous-time models, rather than following the mainstream transformer trend.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to preserve the freedom to explore—to ask questions that might sound a little unusual and give people room to follow them. As you grow, you need more coordination, but you don’t want that coordination to dictate every research direction.

For me, the exciting thing about Sakana is the willingness to look at intelligence through a different lens, especially through ideas from nature and evolution. Keeping that curiosity alive while becoming more disciplined about turning ideas into things that work—that’s the balance I’d like us to maintain.
